conventions.convention: Characters are homomorphisms from a finite abelian group, written additively, to the nonzero complex numbers under multiplication. The dual operation is pointwise multiplication.
The Fourier transform is (F_G f)(χ)=N_R^(-1/2) Σ_x f(x) conjugate(χ(x)), where N_R is the positive canonical real image of |G|. The inverse uses χ(x) without conjugation and the same normalization.
Convolution is (f*g)(z)=Σ_x f(x)g(z-x), with no averaging factor.
H⊥ consists of characters equal to 1 on H; for K contained in the dual, K⊥ consists of group elements on which every character in K equals 1. The pairing is evaluation in both directions.
Parseval uses the counting inner product Σ_x f(x) conjugate(g(x)), linear in the first argument, without division by the index-set cardinality.
An empty product of groups is the trivial group; its character set is a singleton.
Quotients use left cosets, written additively. The annihilator is identified with the quotient dual by inflation and descent.

load_bearing.statement: If G is a finite abelian group with invariant-factor decomposition G ≅ C_n₁ × ⋯ × C_nᵣ, then |Ĝ|=∏ᵢ nᵢ=|G|. The empty product is allowed: it represents the trivial group and has value 1. This is a finite-set cardinality assertion; it does not choose an isomorphism G ≅ Ĝ.
For a finite abelian group G, (F_G f)(χ)=N_R^(-1/2) Σ_{x∈G} f(x) conjugate(χ(x)), where N_R is the canonical positive real image of |G|.
For a subgroup H≤G of a finite abelian group, H⊥ is identified with the character dual of G/H. Consequently |H⊥|=|G/H|=[G:H]=|G|/|H| and |H⊥||H|=|G|.
For a finite abelian group G and x,y∈G, Σ_{χ∈Ĝ} χ(x) conjugate(χ(y)) equals |G| when x=y and 0 otherwise.
The finite coefficient matrix U with entries U_{χ,x}=N_R^(-1/2) conjugate(χ(x)) is square and satisfies U*U=I_G and UU*=I_Ĝ.

A cyclic group C_n=⟨g⟩ of order n≥1 has exactly n additive characters. Evaluation at g bijects these characters with the n distinct complex nth roots of unity; the character corresponding to z is χ_z(jg)=z^j for every integer j.

Restriction to coordinate factors bijects the characters of a finite product of finite abelian groups with the product of their character sets. The inverse sends (χ₁,…,χᵣ) to the character (g₁,…,gᵣ)↦∏ᵢχᵢ(gᵢ); for r=0 both sides are singletons.
For a finite abelian group G, the canonical evaluation map ev:G→Ĝ̂, ev(g)(χ)=χ(g), is a group isomorphism.

For finite abelian G, H≤G and x₀∈G, the transform of 1_{x₀+H} is M_R N_R^(-1/2) conjugate(χ(x₀)) on H⊥ and zero outside. The normalized coset function M_R^(-1/2)1_{x₀+H} has transformed amplitude Q_R^(-1/2) conjugate(χ(x₀)) on H⊥, where M=|H| and Q=|H⊥|.
Let G be a finite abelian group and H≤G. Under the canonical evaluation identification G ≅ Ĝ̂, (H⊥)⊥=H.

concerns.concern: Proof 2.1 writes “|A||H⊥|=|Ĝ|=|G|, the last equality following from [F1].” F1 states the evaluation isomorphism G ≅ Ĝ̂, which directly equates |G| with the double-dual cardinality, not with |Ĝ|. The required equality is available in the theorem cited by F3, whose Statement explicitly includes |Ĝ|=|G|. The argument closes immediately using F3, but the stated attribution to F1 is insufficient.

seams_checked.note: Checked supplier statements against the consuming definitions, sampling algorithm, sample-law F1/F4/F5/F11 and proof, restriction-cut lemma, and common-kernel argument. The QFT uses conjugated characters; normalized coset amplitudes are |H⊥|^(-1/2) conjugate(χ(g)), giving uniform annihilator samples. Recovery uses the proved evaluation and double-annihilator interfaces. Abstract matrix unitarity is explicitly distinguished from encoded-basis orthonormality. The trivial-group branch agrees with the suppliers.

Checked the cyclic-DLP annihilator equation and discrete-log algorithm against cyclic/product character labels, the annihilator definition and the negative-character sampling interface. For H=⟨(-a,1)⟩, membership is exactly d≡ac modulo q, including composite q. The dihedral coset-state lemma separately declares and computes with a positive-sign cyclic QFT; its positive relative phase is consistent with that explicit convention and does not misstate the assigned negative-character transform.
